name: Programmable Settlement and Escrow
title: Programmable Settlement and Escrow
answer: Programmable settlement and escrow covers the use of software rules and smart contracts to hold funds and release them automatically when agreed conditions are met. In payables and receivables it applies to buyer and supplier arrangements, milestone payments, retention on construction contracts, and marketplace transactions where a neutral holding account reduces counterparty risk. The scope includes the trigger logic, the account structure that holds the money, and the reconciliation that follows each release. It sits alongside traditional escrow services and letters of credit rather than replacing them outright.

sections.body: Programmable settlement and escrow covers the use of software rules and smart contracts to hold funds and release them automatically when agreed conditions are met. In payables and receivables it applies to buyer and supplier arrangements, milestone payments, retention on construction contracts, and marketplace transactions where a neutral holding account reduces counterparty risk. The scope includes the trigger logic, the account structure that holds the money, and the reconciliation that follows each release. It sits alongside traditional escrow services and letters of credit rather than replacing them outright.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of conventional banking rails and distributed ledgers. Fiat balances typically sit in a segregated account at a regulated bank or trust company, while the conditions and release instructions are encoded in software that calls payment APIs or smart contracts. Oracles and document feeds supply the evidence that a milestone was met, such as a signed acceptance certificate or a shipping record. Identity and access controls, audit logs, and integration with the ERP or accounts receivable system complete the stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by mapping the commercial agreement into discrete conditions that can be checked by machine or by a named approver. Each condition is tied to a data source, a time window, and a fallback path if the evidence never arrives. The escrow logic is then tested against edge cases such as partial delivery, disputed quality, and early termination before any live funds move. After go live, the team monitors releases, handles exceptions manually where the rules do not fit, and reconciles every movement back to the ledger.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on who controls the account, who can change the rules, and what happens when the parties disagree. Most arrangements keep a regulated institution as escrow agent or custodian, with the software acting as instruction layer rather than as the legal holder of funds. Provenance matters for every trigger: the source of an acceptance signal, the version of the contract logic, and the audit trail of who approved a release. Dispute resolution, chargeback rights, and regulatory treatment of stored value all need to be documented before funds are committed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Adoption is likely to grow where payment terms are already milestone based and where both sides want faster release without giving up protection. Expect more integration between escrow platforms and ERP systems, more use of tokenised deposits inside regulated banking perimeters, and clearer supervisory guidance on when programmable settlement counts as a payment service. The harder problems are legal rather than technical: enforceability of automated release, treatment of errors in the trigger logic, and cross border recognition of digital escrow. Progress will be uneven across jurisdictions and contract types.
